abstract: BACKGROUND: Activation of cell cycle regulatory pathways has been detected during pathological cardiomyocyte growth. However, it has remained unclear whether DNA synthesis pathways play a direct role in cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. We previously discovered in a mouse model of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that there was increased DNA synthesis, which led to cardiomyocyte endoreplication and replication stress–induced DNA damage. We hypothesized that targeting cardiomyocyte endoreplication pathways could reduce pathological myocardial hypertrophy. METHODS: We utilized murine models of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy secondary to mutations in cardiac Mybpc3 (myosin-binding protein C3) −/− or Myh6 (myosin heavy chain 6) R404Q and transverse aortic constriction as a model of pressure overload cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. We manipulated in vivo p21 (cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor 1) protein levels using transgenic mouse models or viral transduction. Cardiomyocyte endoreplication was assessed using flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry of cardiomyocyte nuclei. We also utilized proteomics, proximity ligation assays, and human-induced pluripotent stem cell–derived cardiomyocytes. RESULTS: We discovered that p21 protein peaked during the early stages of hypertrophic growth in both murine hypertrophic cardiomyopathy models and a pressure overload hypertrophy model. Using genetic manipulation of p21 expression, we discovered that cardiomyocyte endoreplication and hypertrophic growth were negatively correlated with p21 expression. Mechanistically, we discovered that p21 bound to PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen), which led to a reduction of PCNA binding to POLD1 (DNA polymerase delta 1). Directly targeting PCNA or POLD1 prevented cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis and hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth. Cardiomyocyte-selective overexpression of p21 using an adeno-associated virus vector reduced long-term pathological left ventricular hypertrophy and improved diastolic function in a preclinical murine model of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Myh6 R404Q ). CONCLUSIONS: Our results demonstrate that PCNA-POLD1–mediated cardiomyocyte endoreplication drives hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth, and p21 serves as a negative regulator of this process. Targeting these pathways demonstrates therapeutic potential in preventing pathological myocardial hypertrophy.

Murine Echocardiography and Transverse Aortic Constriction
Murine transthoracic echocardiography was performed using Vevo 2100 and 3100 High-Resolution system (VisualSonics, Inc). Under conscious conditions, left ventricular (LV) posterior wall at end-diastole, septal thickness at end-diastole, LV internal dimensions at end-diastole, and LV internal dimensions at end-systole were measured from the 2-dimensional M-mode images. Under anesthesia, LV diastolic function was measured in B-mode apical 4-chamber view. LV filling peak velocity (E) and atrial contraction flow peak velocity (A) were obtained by mitral valve Doppler flow. Early (E’) and late (A′) diastolic mitral annular motion velocity was obtained by tissue Doppler imaging. Isovolumic relaxation time was determined as the interval between aortic valve closure and mitral valve opening.
Transverse aortic constriction (TAC) was performed in the dedicated facility at the University of Pittsburgh. Eight- to 9-week-old mice were used for the surgery. Echocardiography was performed before and 6 weeks after the surgery. Post-procedure, transaortic gradients were measured using echocardiography to assess satisfactory aortic constriction. Investigators were blinded to the genotype or grouping of mice during all measurements. Please see the
Supplemental Methods
for additional details.

Novelty and Significance
What Is Known?
Increased cardiomyocyte DNA content has been detected in multiple forms of pathological myocardial remodeling.
Activation of cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis pathways and endoreplication has been detected in mice deficient in the sarcomere protein Mybpc3 (myosin-binding protein C3) during the earliest stages of cardiac remodeling.
It remained unclear whether cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis was a direct regulator of cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and whether targeting this pathway could improve pathological myocardial remodeling and ventricular function.
What New Information Does This Article Contribute?
Murine models of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pressure overload show an induction of cardiomyocyte p21 (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1) during the earliest stages of hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth, and p21 expression is negatively correlated with cardiomyocyte DNA content and hypertrophy.
Cardiomyocyte p21 binds to PCNA (proliferating cell nuclear antigen), which causes reduced PCNA interactions with the key DNA synthesis polymerase POLD1 (DNA polymerase delta 1), and this leads to decreased cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis and hypertrophic growth in both murine and human cardiomyocytes.
Activation of DNA synthesis pathways is a critical event in hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth, and targeting these pathways can reduce pathological myocardial remodeling and improve left ventricular diastolic function in a preclinical model of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Induction of cardiomyocyte cell cycle regulatory pathways has been identified in multiple different forms of pathological myocardial remodeling. However, it has remained unclear whether DNA synthesis pathways play an active role in regulating hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth. Using both genetic and pressure overload murine models, we observed an increase in nuclear p21 protein concentrations during the initial stages of hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth. Genetic reduction or overexpression of p21 revealed a negative correlation between cardiomyocyte p21 levels and cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis and hypertrophy. Mechanistically, cardiomyocyte p21 binds to PCNA, which leads to reduced PCNA interactions with the crucial DNA synthesis polymerase POLD1. This causes decreased cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis and hypertrophic growth in both murine and human cardiomyocytes. Targeting these pathways can reduce pathological myocardial hypertrophy and improve left ventricular diastolic function in a preclinical murine model of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Overall, this study identified a conserved role for PCNA-POLD1–controlled cardiomyocyte endoreplication as an important regulator of pathological cardiomyocyte growth and identified p21 as a key negative regulator of this pathway.

Endoreplication occurs when nuclear DNA (nDNA) synthesis takes place without subsequent cytokinesis, leading to cellular multinucleation and polyploidy.
1
–
3
This process occurs in cells from a wide range of fungi, plants, and animal species and is thought to serve a role in normal developmental growth and to protect cells from pathological stressors. Malignant cells also undergo endoreplication, and there is evidence that this process provides these cells a survival advantage from genotoxic stress.
4
–
6
During normal heart development, postnatal mammalian cardiomyocytes transition from hyperplastic to hypertrophic growth.
7
During this transition to hypertrophic growth, there is a period when endoreplication takes place, which leads to cardiomyocyte multinucleation and polyploidy. Changes in cardiomyocyte polyploidy have been reported as a regulator of cardiomyocyte proliferation across multiple vertebrate species.
8
–
10
However, when methods to reduce polyploidy have been attempted in adult murine cardiomyocytes, there was not a robust increase in cardiomyocyte proliferation.
11
,
12
Therefore, it remains unclear whether increased DNA content directly impairs mammalian cardiomyocyte cytokinesis.
In contrast to normal cardiomyocyte growth during heart development, pathological cardiomyocyte hypertrophy is associated with a multitude of changes in cardiomyocyte gene expression, signaling, and metabolism that lead to increased risk of cardiomyopathy and heart failure.
13
In addition to normal postnatal development, activation of adult cardiomyocyte cell cycle activity and increased cardiomyocyte polyploidy have been detected in both human and mouse myocardial tissue exposed to pathological stimuli.
11
,
14
–
23
However, it has remained unclear whether increased cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis is a direct cause of pathological cardiomyocyte growth or is a secondary response to the hypertrophic growth process. A transgenic mouse model that overexpressed Myc in adult mouse cardiomyocytes induced hypertrophic growth and increased cardiomyocyte cell cycle activity secondary to upregulation of the cell cycle stimulatory protein, cyclin D2.
24
,
25
However, in vitro experiments targeting the CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase) 2 and CDK4 suggested that the Myc-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophic growth may be independent of the cyclin D2 induction of DNA synthesis.
25
Likewise, not all studies have detected increased cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis during pathological myocardial remodeling.
26
,
27
In addition, gene expression in cardiomyocytes with different levels of multinucleation or nuclear ploidy is reported to be divergent in some studies but similar in others.
18
,
28
,
29
Therefore, it remains incompletely understood if changes in DNA synthesis directly facilitate pathological cardiomyocyte growth and the endogenous mechanisms regulating this process.
Previously, in a murine model of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM; Mybpc3 [myosin-binding protein C3]
−/−
), we discovered that there was increased cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis during the early postnatal time period, which led to increased cardiomyocyte endoreplication.
30
Subsequent studies have shown that this increased cell cycle activity led to replication stress–induced DNA damage and activation of the DNA damage response pathways with a surge in gene expression of Cdkn1a (CDK inhibitor 1a), which codes for the protein p21 (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 1).
31
We hypothesized that cardiomyocyte endoreplication was critical for pathological cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, and p21 served as a negative regulator of this pathway. To test this hypothesis, we utilized gain and loss of function murine models and human iPS–derived cardiomyocytes to define the molecular mechanisms regulating cardiomyocyte endoreplication and pathological cell growth.

Discussion
We previously discovered increased cardiomyocyte endoreplication and replication stress during the early stages of pathological remodeling in murine models of HCM.
30
,
31
However, it remained unclear whether cardiomyocyte endoreplication was directly involved in hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth, and the molecular mechanisms regulating this process remained poorly defined. In this study, we identified a surge of p21 during the early hypertrophic growth phase in the Mybpc3
−/−
murine HCM model. Genetic reduction of p21 in this model led to a dramatic increase in cardiomyocyte endoreplication and hypertrophic growth. In contrast, amplification of cardiomyocyte p21 reduced cardiomyocyte endoreplication and hypertrophy. Utilizing murine models and human cardiomyocytes, we discovered that p21 bound to the DNA clamp protein PCNA. The increased p21-PCNA protein interactions led to a reduction of PCNA binding to the key DNA synthesis polymerase POLD1. Directly targeting PCNA or POLD1 reduced cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis and pathological hypertrophic growth. We utilized the Myh6
R404Q/WT
HCM model and TAC pressure overload model to show that the induction of PCNA-POLD1–regulated cardiomyocyte endoreplication is conserved across multiple different forms of pathological cardiomyocyte hypertrophy. Likewise, these models allowed us to determine that the activation of pathological cardiomyocyte endoreplication precedes the development of cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and is not a response to hypertrophic growth. Last, the viral overexpression of cardiomyocyte p21 in the Myh6
R404Q/WT
HCM model reduced the development of LVH and normalized ventricular diastolic function, highlighting the therapeutic potential of targeting this pathway. Taken together, this study revealed a conserved role for PCNA-POLD1–regulated cardiomyocyte endoreplication as a key driver of pathological cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and establishes p21 as an important negative regulator of this process (Figure
8
Q).
DNA Synthesis Pathways Regulating Cardiomyocyte Hypertrophic Growth
Increases in cardiomyocyte multinucleation and polyploidy are a common finding in pathological heart growth.
11
,
14
–
23
However, it remained unclear whether cardiomyocyte nDNA synthesis pathways directly regulate pathological cardiomyocyte growth. For example, experiments that overexpressed the transcription factor Myc in cardiomyocytes induced DNA synthesis and hypertrophic growth.
25
However, inhibition of CDK2 was unable to prevent the increased cardiomyocyte growth despite a reduction in Myc-induced cardiomyocyte DNA synthesis.
25
We utilized in vivo gain and loss of function experiments to identify p21 as an endogenous inhibitor of cardiomyocyte endoreplication and pathological cardiomyocyte growth. Endoreplication occurs across a wide range of cell types in both plants and animals, and there is a consistent correlation between nuclear and cell size.
41
However, it remains largely unknown how endoreplication regulates cell growth. Mechanistically, we discovered that cardiomyocyte p21 binds to the DNA clamp PCNA, which leads to reduced binding of PCNA to the key DNA synthesis enzyme POLD1. The interaction of PCNA and POLD1 is a key component of lagging-strand DNA synthesis across eukaryotes and is critical for cell proliferation.
38
,
39
,
42
,
43
Likewise, it is well established that p21 can inhibit PCNA and POLD1 binding in vitro.
40
Our results show that PCNA-POLD1 protein interactions are also important in mediating nonproliferative hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth through regulation of endoreplication, and p21 serves as an endogenous negative regulator of this process in the heart. Interestingly, in proliferating cells from plants, yeast, and humans, it has been shown that increased cell size induces cell cycle activators or decreases cell cycle inhibitors to stimulate cell cycle progression and cell division to maintain a constant cell size.
44
–
47
Our results show that nonproliferating cell types such as cardiomyocytes also regulate the cell cycle in an effort to control cellular growth. In contrast to proliferating cells where activation of the cell cycle stimulates cell division, we found that activation of the cell cycle in postnatal cardiomyocytes leads to endoreplication and hypertrophic cell growth, and p21 serves as a key negative regulator of this process.
Our results show that cardiomyocyte endoreplication pathways are induced at the earliest stages of pathological hypertrophic growth in both genetic and pressure overload murine models. Importantly, we have shown the translational potential of targeting these pathways using a gene therapy approach to prevent the development of myocardial hypertrophy and LV diastolic dysfunction in the Myh6
R404Q
HCM model. In contrast to the Myh6
R404Q/WT
model, which has primarily concentric myocardial hypertrophy similar to human HCM, the Mybpc3
−/−
model has features consistent with both concentric hypertrophy (increased wall thickening) and eccentric remodeling (increased LV dilation). We found that elimination of cardiomyocyte p21 in this model caused a massive increase in concentric myocardial hypertrophy that persisted as the animals aged. In contrast, we found that cardiomyocyte p21 overexpression in Mybpc3
−/−
mice reduced concentric myocardial hypertrophy, but, as the animals aged, they developed evidence of increased eccentric LV remodeling with a reduction in LV wall thickness and a trend toward increased LV end diastolic diameter. At this time, we do not know whether this aging-associated eccentric LV remodeling is secondary to a reduction of the initial cardiomyocyte hypertrophic response or another factor unique to the Mybpc3
−/−
model. Importantly, in our TAC model of pathological hypertrophy that used the same Myh6Cre/Cdkn1a
SUPER
method to selectively increase cardiomyocyte p21, we did not detect any increase in LV eccentric remodeling. Likewise, we did not detect evidence of eccentric LV remodeling in the Myh6
R404Q/WT
model injected with the AAV9-cTnT-Cdkn1a vector. Overall, results from this study provide potential molecular mechanisms for why gene-targeting approaches for HCM in preclinical murine models are successful at preventing disease but have reduced efficacy in reversing established disease.
48
–
52
To optimize the translational potential of targeting these pathways, it will be critical to identify the shared and divergent responses in different preclinical animal models and humans with pathological hypertrophic remodeling.
53
p21 and Ventricular Hypertrophic Remodeling
We discovered that p21 protein levels increased during the earliest stages of pathological cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in both genetic and acquired cardiomyopathy models, and our results define p21 as a negative regulator of cardiomyocyte hypertrophy through inhibition of DNA synthesis–induced endoreplication. Interestingly, multiple human genetic studies have identified associations between single-nucleotide polymorphisms associated with the gene that encodes p21, Cdkn1a, and changes in human LV structure and function.
54
–
58
Three of these Cdkn1a single-nucleotide polymorphisms were specifically associated with increased risk of developing myocardial hypertrophy or HCM (rs146170154, rs3176326, and rs66761782).
54
,
55
,
58
These human genome wide association studies (GWAS) studies and our mechanistic studies highlight the important role that p21 has in regulating pathological myocardial hypertrophy across species. It will be interesting to determine how these single-nucleotide polymorphisms impact cardiomyocyte Cdkn1a gene expression and endoreplication pathways.
Similar to our results in cardiomyocytes, p21 has been shown to negatively regulate polyploidization across other cell types such as megakaryocytes, hepatocytes, and hematopoietic cells.
59
–
62
Previously, we found that the induction of p21 in hypertrophic cardiomyocytes was secondary to increased DNA damage caused by replication stress.
31
Interestingly, early postnatal telomere dysfunction secondary to telomerase deficiency has been shown to increase cardiomyocyte p21, and this induction of p21 negatively regulates early postnatal cardiomyocyte proliferation.
63
Our results show that at later developmental time points, p21 maintains its role as a negative regulator of the cardiomyocyte cell cycle, but it regulates cardiomyocyte hypertrophic growth and not proliferation.
We found that p21 protein levels were preferentially increased in the cardiomyocyte nucleus in our in vivo HCM model. In contrast, an earlier study reported that cytoplasmic p21 levels increased in cultured neonatal rat cardiomyocytes exposed to lovastatin, which led to binding of p21 to ρ-associated protein kinase (ROCK1 [Rho-associated protein kinase 1]), and this was proposed as the mechanism through which lovastatin reduced angiotensin II–induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy.
64
The different cellular localizations of p21 in our study versus the neonatal rat cardiomyocyte study may be related to the models studied or the hypertrophic stimuli utilized. Of note, we did not detect evidence of p21 binding to ROCK1 or 2 kinases in our proteomics screen, which suggests that different molecular mechanisms are likely occurring. In a second study, utilizing angiotensin II as a hypertrophic stimulus, it was shown that total myocardial p21 levels decreased after angiotensin II stimulation.
65
In contrast, we found that nuclear p21 levels were increased at the early stages of both genetic and pressure overload hypertrophic stimuli. Interestingly, it was reported that CDK2 and CDK4 activity and phosphorylation of Rb (retinoblastoma protein) were reduced after increasing p21 protein levels in a non-cell type–specific manner by injecting a modified p21 peptide.
65
However, cardiomyocyte cell cycle activity and ploidy were not measured in that study, and the method utilized to increase myocardial p21 levels was not cardiomyocyte-selective. Therefore, it was unclear whether the reported molecular changes were related to changes in cardiomyocyte or noncardiomyocyte cell populations. Our results indicate that during the earliest stages of hypertrophic growth, p21 does have increased binding to CDK2. However, p21 binding to PCNA is greater during that time period. Importantly, we identified that p21 reduces cardiomyocyte hypertrophic growth through direct inhibition of PCNA and POLD1-induced endoreplication and not through a potential non-cell cycle–related activity of CDKs.
Senescence and p21
In cell populations that proliferate throughout different stages of development, the induction of p21 coincides with cessation of cell proliferation and is often used as a marker of cellular senescence.
66
Proliferative arrest is a key feature of many senescent cell populations. However, proliferative arrest cannot be used as a marker of senescence in cell populations that are primarily nonproliferative such as cardiomyocytes. During aging, it has been reported that p21 and p16 protein levels are increased in cardiomyocytes secondary to age-related telomere damage, and it has been shown that senolytics can reduce age-related myocardial hypertrophy.
67
Although we detect a large increase in cardiomyocyte p21 protein levels secondary to increased cardiomyocyte DNA damage, our previous studies determined that replication stress and not telomere damage were the causes of the increased p21 expression.
31
These results suggest that although induction of p21 is often associated with cellular senescence, other factors are contributing to the transition to a senescent cellular phenotype. Supporting this are experiments from p21-deficient fibroblasts, which identified a transition to a senescent cellular phenotype despite the absence of p21 protein.
68
Studies have shown that cardiomyocyte senescence leads to increased pathological myocardial remodeling with aging or ischemic injury and methods to target senescence blunt some aspects of the pathological myocardial remodeling process.
67
,
69
,
70
However, the role of senescence in regulating cardiomyocyte hypertrophy is less clear because targeting myocardial senescence in a non-cell type–selective manner reduced aging-related cardiomyocyte hypertrophy but did not reduce cardiomyocyte hypertrophy secondary to ischemia reperfusion.
67
,
69
Likewise, our results demonstrate that increasing cardiomyocyte p21 levels reduces pathological hypertrophic cardiomyocyte growth and can improve LV diastolic function. Taken together, these results suggest that the induction of p21 and the impact it has on regulating cardiomyocyte growth may be context and disease-dependent.
Conclusions
We have utilized multiple models of myocardial hypertrophy to define a unique role for PCNA and POLD1 in regulating cardiomyocyte endoreplication and pathological growth. This study has identified a critical role for DNA synthesis pathways in regulating adult cardiomyocyte pathological growth and defined the key molecular mechanisms controlling this process.
